name: Blue and John Crow Mountains National Park
blurb: Misty Jamaican peaks where tree ferns, fruit bats and the giant swallowtail meet the boa.

tip.title: Thin the Ocotea trees
tip.text: Ocotea trees give fruit to hutias, bats and pigeons and are a place the giant swallowtail lays eggs. Set Ocotea to -100% and watch those animals, then the Jamaican boa.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blue and John Crow Mountains National Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Ocotea trees
nodes.desc: Laurel-family forest trees. Female giant swallowtails have been seen laying eggs on Ocotea, and the trees bear fruit that forest animals eat.
A flowering shrub whose nectar is used by the Homerus swallowtail. Hummingbirds and other nectar feeders also visit it.
Eats mainly fruit, especially figs, and carries it away to eat, which spreads seeds through the forest.
A small nectar and fruit eater. It pierces flower bases to reach nectar, which other nectar feeders then use.

nodes.name: Jamaican forest frogs
nodes.desc: Several small frog species recorded in the park that develop without a tadpole stage. They hunt small invertebrates on the forest floor.
An introduced predator on Jamaica that eats small lizards, frogs and ground-nesting birds, and so competes with native predators.
Called the John crow in Jamaica, which gave the mountains half of their name. It scavenges carrion.
Heavy rain and constant mist keep humidity high. This is the main driver of the mountain's lush forest.
Light reaching the forest canopy and clearings drives growth of trees, ferns and flowering shrubs.
Nutrient-rich soil and leaf litter feed the forest plants, topped up by decomposers.
Fungi, bacteria and litter invertebrates break down dead leaves, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
